output.title: When opt-in records stop being trustworthy
output.body:
If your opt-in records stop being trustworthy, treat it as a workflow check before the next send, not as a broad AI project. The question is simple: can you tell, for each contact, whether consent is current, withdrawn, or unclear? If you cannot, do not guess.

For a small business owner, this usually shows up as manual checking, a spreadsheet full of edge cases, or the habit of sending to a list because it is there. That is where the time leak starts. In the approved persona scenario, repetitive manual work is already a meaningful drag; consent checks can become part of that same drag if the records are messy. Keep the 8–10 hour figure in its original persona context: repeated customer questions, neglected leads, and manual invoice/data work. It is not a measured cost of consent checking.

One practical next step: before the next campaign, mark every contact as current, stale, or unknown based on the evidence you already have, then route the stale and unknown group away from the send list. That can be manual, spreadsheet-based, or automation-assisted depending on your tooling. If your email system already keeps consent history or lets you segment cleanly, use that as the first diagnostic. If it does not, a small workflow check in your own environment may be enough to expose the gap. Human approval still stays in the loop for any send decision. A boring list review is still better than a polite mistake.
